newsitem.title: CHINA: West accused of trying to divide China.
newsitem.headline: West accused of trying to divide China.

text.p: China's propaganda machine has accused the West of using the restive region of Xinjiang as a tool to try to Westernise and break up China in the post-Cold War era.

"After drastic changes in Eastern Europe and the disintegration of the Soviet Union, hostile Western forces have intensified (their campaign) to Westernise and disintegrate China," the official Xinjiang Daily said in an edition seen in Beijing on Monday.

"Hostile Western forces... have tried to look for and open points of penetration in our border areas inhabited by ethnic minorities. Xinjiang is one of their points of penetration," the newspaper said.
The separatist activities of the ethnic minorities had the support of hostile Western forces and exiled pro-independence groups, it said, without identifying the hostile Western forces.

Three bombs planted on buses blew up within minutes of each other in Xinjiang's capital Urumqi on February 25 in an apparently coordinated attack that coincided with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
The bombings killed nine and wounded 74.
Seven people have been arrested, a Beijing-funded Hong Kong newspaper has said.

Exiled ethnic Uighurs, who want to set up an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, have claimed responsibility for the bombings and vowed to stage more attacks until they gain "complete freedom" for their Moslem homeland.
The official Xinjiang Daily newspaper said independence for the region was out of the question and authorities should show no pity for separatists.
"The political goal of separatists is to overthrow the Communist Party... split Xinjiang from the big family of the motherland," the newspaper said.
"There is no room for compromise on this question of political principles and we absolutely cannot compromise.
"Their crimes are barbaric and seriously endanger national security and reunification," it said. "We should not be softhearted... merciful toward them."

In February, an anti-Chinese riot erupted in the town of Yining in far-western Xinjiang. Nine people were killed and 198 injured in the unrest -- one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.
"It (unrest)... is neither an ethnic nor a religious problem. Separatists are the common enemy of the people," the newspaper said.
Chinese officials have said there was no evidence linking the Urumqi attacks with a similar bombing in Beijing in March.

Beijing police have, however, called on hotels to strengthen security and asked taxi drivers in the Chinese capital not to give rides to suspicious-looking people from Xinjiang and to be especially cautious in neighbourhoods where many Uighur migrants live.
Beijing also faces sporadic outbursts of anti-Chinese unrest in Tibet, where monks and nuns are often at the forefront of demonstrations for independence.

China blames the Dalai Lama, the Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader who fled into exile in India after an abortive uprising against communist rule in 1959, and his followers for the unrest in the Himalayan region.
The Dalai Lama, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989, says he wants autonomy and freedom of worship in his deeply Buddhist homeland.
